nameStory: The brown widow gets its name from its brownish coloration, distinguishing it from its more famous black widow cousins. Like all widow spiders, females of this species were once believed to always eat their mates after breeding, though this actually happens less often than folklore suggests.
description: The brown widow is a medium-sized spider with a rounded abdomen that's typically tan to brown in color with distinctive black and white patterns along the sides. Females are larger than males and sport the classic widow hourglass marking on their belly, though theirs is orange-yellow rather than bright red. These spiders build irregular, tangled webs in sheltered spots and are relatively new arrivals to New England, with only a handful of confirmed sightings so far.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the orange-yellow hourglass shape on the underside of the rounded abdomen, plus distinctive black and white geometric patterns running along the sides of the belly that look like angular stripes or chevrons.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Females have a distinctly bulbous, almost marble-shaped abdomen that feels firm if gently touched, while males are much smaller and more elongated with thinner abdomens.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates messy, irregular webs that feel sticky and substantial to the touch, typically built in corners of structures, under eaves, or in cluttered areas like sheds and garages.

idTips.label: Egg Sacs
idTips.description: Produces distinctive round egg sacs covered in small spiky projections that make them feel rough and bumpy, like tiny sea urchins - this is unique among widow spiders.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Adult females reach about the size of a marble including legs, while males are roughly half that size and much more slender in build.

habitat: Brown widows prefer warm, sheltered locations around human structures like garages, sheds, outdoor furniture, and under building overhangs. In New England's climate, they're most likely to survive in heated buildings or very protected outdoor spots that stay relatively warm year-round.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, with females beginning to produce their characteristic spiky egg sacs in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most noticeable and egg sacs are commonly found. This is the best time to spot adults in their webs.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues in warm weather, but begins to decline as temperatures drop. Late-season egg sacs may be observed.
seasonality.winter: In New England's harsh winters, brown widows typically only survive in heated indoor spaces or very protected microhabitats.

funFact: Brown widow egg sacs look like tiny medieval maces covered in spikes - these projections are completely unique among North American widow spiders and make identification foolproof even when you can't see the spider itself!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with black widows, but brown widows have that distinctive orange-yellow hourglass (not bright red) and geometric black-and-white side patterns that black widows lack. Remember: orange hourglass = brown widow, red hourglass = black widow.
contextualKnowledge: Brown widows are considered an invasive species that's expanding northward due to climate change and global trade. Despite being venomous widows, their bites are generally less medically significant than those of black widows, though any widow bite should still be taken seriously.
compareHints: Unlike the solid black coloration of black widows, brown widows display intricate geometric patterns in black and white along their sides. The hourglass marking is also distinctly orange-yellow rather than the bright red seen in both Northern and Southern black widows. Brown widows also produce those uniquely spiky egg sacs that neither black widow species creates.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Northern Black Widow differs from the Southern Black Widow primarily in its geographic range and cold tolerance - southerns rarely venture this far north.
The Southern Black Widow's complete red hourglass marking distinguishes it from the Northern Black Widow's broken hourglass pattern.
